---
title: "AMLab — measurement science on an Arduino"
subtitle: "Laboratory activities for courses in measurement science and technology"
toc: false
---

AMLab is a set of laboratory activities built on
[ArduinoDriver](https://github.com/pbosetti/ArduinoDriver), which turns a
supported Arduino board into a USB vendor-class I/O device: digital I/O,
analog input, PWM, DAC, timestamped bulk-endpoint streaming, pin events and a
device clock, driven from a host computer through a C++20 library, the
`arduino-io` command line tool, or the Python and R bindings.

The point of the platform, for a measurement course, is that the board is
*honest about its own limits*. Every stream record carries the device's own
`micros()` timestamp, lost records are counted rather than hidden, and the
board reports its own ADC resolution, reference voltage and capabilities. That
makes it possible to teach the whole chain — sensor, conditioning, conversion,
sampling, estimation, uncertainty — on a bench that costs a fraction of a
commercial DAQ.

## Who this is for

::: {.grid}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Students

Each experiment gives you a short introductory presentation, a handbook with
the theory and the bench procedure, and two analysis templates — one in
Python, one in R — that you fill in with your own measurements. Every
experiment ends with an uncertainty budget: a measurement without one is an
opinion.

[Start with an experiment →](experiments/index.qmd)
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### Instructors

The same sources build an instructor edition with expected results, common
pitfalls, session timing and assessment rubrics. Setup pages cover firmware,
host operating systems and the two language bindings; hardware pages describe
the conditioning and filter stages, the thermal rig and the beam rig, with a
bill of materials per cost tier.

[Prepare a bench →](setup/index.qmd)
:::

:::

## How the material is organised

| Section | What it holds |
|---|---|
| [Setup](setup/index.qmd) | Boards, firmware, host operating systems, Python and R bindings, a verification procedure and troubleshooting |
| [Hardware](hardware/index.qmd) | Signal conditioning, anti-alias filtering, the thermal rig, the cantilever beam rig, bill of materials |
| [Data format](data-format/index.qmd) | One CSV + YAML sidecar convention for every acquisition, and the `labtools` readers |
| [Experiments](experiments/index.qmd) | Nine experiments in three strands: DAQ characterization, thermal, mechanical |

Every experiment ships **reference data** generated by seeded synthetic
generators, so the analysis templates render — and are checked in continuous
integration — with no hardware attached. Synthetic data is labelled as such on
every page that uses it.

::: {.callout-important}
## Host operating system is an influence quantity

Sampling is driven by the sketch's `loop()`, not by a hardware timer, and the
host's USB scheduling shapes what actually arrives. On Linux the jitter
observed on the reference bench is typically 1–2 µs; on macOS schedule
restarts and device overruns are more common. The recommended lab host is
Linux — one small machine per bench, a Raspberry Pi is enough. This is a
property of the platform, and the experiments measure it rather than hide it.
:::
